text: {"explain":"Spanish vowels are short and pure: a, e, i, o, u sound like आ, ए, ई, ओ, ऊ but never glide. The h is silent, so hola is 'ola'. J is a strong English h, so trabajo is 'trabaho'. Ñ is like the ny in canyon, so mañana is 'manyana'. In Peru, ll sounds like English y, so me llamo is 'me yamo'. Single r between vowels is a quick tap, as in pero. Most words ending in a vowel, n or s stress the second-to-last syllable, so trabajo stresses 'ba'. An accent mark like reunión shows an exception.","items":[{"type":"mcq","q":"How is the h in hola pronounced?","options":["As a breathy h, like in Hindi हाथ","Silent, so hola sounds like 'ola'","As a hard k, like in English 'kola'","As a long vowel, like 'oola'"],"answer":"Silent, so hola sounds like 'ola'","why":"In Spanish the letter h is always silent, so hola is pronounced 'ola'."},{"type":"mcq","q":"How does the j in trabajo sound?","options":["Like the j in English 'jump'","Like a strong English h","Like the Hindi ज in जल","Like a silent letter"],"answer":"Like a strong English h","why":"Spanish j is a strong, breathy h sound, so trabajo begins with a clear h-like sound."},{"type":"mcq","q":"Which sound is closest to the ñ in mañana?","options":["The n in English 'net'","The ny in English 'canyon'","The ng in English 'sing'","The double n in English 'unnamed'"],"answer":"The ny in English 'canyon'","why":"Spanish ñ is a distinct letter with the ny sound of canyon, not plain n."},{"type":"mcq","q":"Where is the stress in trabajo?","options":["On the first syllable, 'TRA'","On the second-to-last syllable, 'ba'","On the last syllable, 'jo'","Equal stress on every syllable"],"answer":"On the second-to-last syllable, 'ba'","why":"Words ending in a vowel stress the second-to-last syllable, so trabajo is tra-BA-jo."},{"type":"recall","q":"In Peru, how do you pronounce the ll in me llamo, and how do you pronounce the single r in pero?","answer":"ll sounds like English y, so me llamo is 'me yamo'. Single r between vowels is a quick tap, like the र in पर.","why":"Peruvian Spanish uses the y sound for ll, and a single r between vowels is a quick tap."},{"type":"recall","q":"Say the word mañana aloud, then state which syllable is stressed and why.","answer":"man-YA-na, with stress on the second-to-last syllable 'ña', because it ends in a vowel.","why":"Words ending in a vowel, n or s stress the second-to-last syllable, and mañana follows this pattern."}]}

{"explain":"Python finds many mistakes only when a line runs. Rust checks types before the program runs, so a mismatch stops the build. Cargo is Rust's combined tool: it creates projects (cargo new), compiles and runs them (cargo run), and manages dependencies, like pip, venv, and a build tool in one. Variables are immutable by default, so let x = 5; x = 6; fails, while let mut x = 5; x = 6; works. Function parameters and non-unit return types must be typed: fn add(a: i32, b: i32) -> i32 { a + b } returns a + b because the final expression has no semicolon. Adding a semicolon there would make the function return nothing, which fails to compile.","items":[{"type":"mcq","q":"Which command type-checks a Cargo project without producing a final binary?","options":["cargo run","cargo check","cargo new","cargo build --release"],"answer":"cargo check","why":"cargo check runs the type checker only, while cargo run compiles and also executes the program."},{"type":"mcq","q":"What does let x = 5; x = 6; produce in Rust?","options":["A compile error, because x is immutable by default","A runtime panic when x is reassigned","A silent overwrite, as in Python","A warning, and x becomes 6"],"answer":"A compile error, because x is immutable by default","why":"Variables declared with let are immutable unless marked mut, and the compiler rejects the reassignment before the program runs."},{"type":"mcq","q":"Given fn double(n: i32) -> i32 { n * 2; }, what happens?","options":["It returns n * 2 as expected","It fails to compile because the body returns nothing","It returns 0 at runtime","It compiles but returns n unchanged"],"answer":"It fails to compile because the body returns nothing","why":"The semicolon turns the final expression into a statement, so the block's value is unit, which conflicts with the declared i32 return type."},{"type":"mcq","q":"Which file does cargo new create alongside Cargo.toml?","options":["src/lib.rs","src/main.rs","main.py","build.rs"],"answer":"src/main.rs","why":"cargo new creates a binary project with src/main.rs as its entry point."},{"type":"recall","q":"Explain the difference between let mut x = 5; and shadowing with let x = x + 1; in one or two sentences.","answer":"let mut x = 5 creates one variable that can be reassigned later with x = ..., keeping its type. Shadowing with a new let creates a new variable that reuses the name, and it may have a different type, such as turning a string into an integer.","why":"The two look similar but differ in mutability and in whether a new variable is created, which the lesson covers as a key distinction."},{"type":"recall","q":"In Python, a type hint like def f(x: int) doesn't stop a wrong argument from running. What does Rust do differently for a function with fn f(x: i32)?","answer":"Rust always checks the types at compile time, so passing a value of the wrong type is rejected before the program runs.","why":"This contrasts Python's unenforced hints with Rust's always-checked static types, which is the core idea of the lesson."}]}

{"explain":"Greet by time of day: Buenos días (morning), Buenas tardes (afternoon), Buenas noches (evening or goodnight). Ask how someone is with ¿Cómo estás? (tú, informal) or ¿Cómo está usted? (formal). Use usted with clients and senior people until they invite tú, then mirror your coworkers. Reply with Bien, gracias. ¿Y tú? or ¿Y usted? Mañana means tomorrow, so Hasta mañana means See you tomorrow. Example: Buenos días, Carlos. ¿Cómo está usted? Bien, gracias. ¿Y usted? To address a group, use ustedes.","items":[{"type":"mcq","q":"Which greeting fits best at 9 a.m. with a coworker?","options":["Buenos días","Buenas tardes","Buenas noches","Hasta mañana"],"answer":"Buenos días","why":"Buenos días means good morning, so it suits the morning."},{"type":"mcq","q":"What does Hasta mañana mean?","options":["See you tomorrow","See you later today","Good morning to you","See you this evening"],"answer":"See you tomorrow","why":"Mañana means tomorrow, so Hasta mañana means See you tomorrow."},{"type":"mcq","q":"Which question is correct when greeting a senior client, Mr. Ruiz?","options":["¿Cómo está usted?","¿Cómo estás?","¿Cómo estás tú?","¿Cómo estamos?"],"answer":"¿Cómo está usted?","why":"Usted takes the formal form está, which suits a senior client."},{"type":"mcq","q":"A client asks ¿Cómo está usted? Which reply is correct?","options":["Bien, gracias. ¿Y usted?","Bien, gracias. ¿Y tú?","Buenas noches, gracias.","Hasta mañana, gracias."],"answer":"Bien, gracias. ¿Y usted?","why":"When the client uses usted, you reply with usted and ask ¿Y usted?"},{"type":"recall","q":"Say a greeting for 3 p.m. to a coworker, then ask how they are and give the reply that asks them back.","answer":"Buenas tardes. ¿Cómo estás? Bien, gracias. ¿Y tú?","why":"Buenas tardes fits the afternoon, and ¿Cómo estás? is the informal tú question."},{"type":"recall","q":"Write Spanish for See you tomorrow, then say which word means tomorrow.","answer":"Hasta mañana. Mañana means tomorrow.","why":"Hasta mañana is the farewell, and mañana is the word for tomorrow, not today."}]}

{"explain":"In Spanish, you introduce yourself with me llamo, which literally means 'I call myself'. Me is not 'my'. It is a reflexive word that goes with llamar. Mi means 'my' and always comes before a noun, as in mi nombre (my name). So say Me llamo Alex or Mi nombre es Alex, never Mi llamo. To ask a coworker's name informally, say ¿Cómo te llamas? To ask a senior client formally, say ¿Cómo se llama? Reply with Mucho gusto (Nice to meet you). A woman adds Encantada, and a man says Encantado. Practise aloud: Me llamo ___.","items":[{"type":"mcq","q":"Which sentence correctly says 'My name is Alex'?","options":["Mi llamo Alex","Me llamo Alex","Me nombre es Alex","Yo llamo Alex"],"answer":"Me llamo Alex","why":"Me llamo is the reflexive 'I call myself' pattern, while mi is only used before a noun."},{"type":"mcq","q":"In the phrase mi nombre, what does mi mean?","options":["my","me","I","your"],"answer":"my","why":"Mi is a possessive meaning 'my' and goes before a noun like nombre."},{"type":"mcq","q":"Which question asks a coworker their name informally?","options":["¿Cómo te llamas?","¿Cómo se llama?","¿Cómo me llamo?","¿Cómo llamas?"],"answer":"¿Cómo te llamas?","why":"Te llamas is the informal form used with a coworker, while se llama is formal."},{"type":"mcq","q":"Which word should a woman say to mean 'pleased to meet you'?","options":["Encantada","Encantado","Encantador","Encantar"],"answer":"Encantada","why":"Encantada is the feminine form a woman uses, while encantado is for men."},{"type":"recall","q":"Introduce yourself in one Spanish sentence using me llamo, with your own name or a made-up one.","answer":"Me llamo [name], for example: Me llamo Priya.","why":"This practises the correct me llamo pattern and avoids the mi llamo mistake."},{"type":"recall","q":"In one sentence, explain why Mi llamo is wrong and what the correct form is.","answer":"Mi means 'my' and needs a noun after it, but llamo needs the reflexive me, so the correct form is Me llamo.","why":"This checks that the learner understands the difference between mi and me and why me llamo is used."}]}

{"explain":"In Python, changing a list while looping over it can silently skip items, and nothing warns you. Rust catches conflicting access at compile time. A reference is a borrow. &T is a shared reference that only reads, so you cannot mutate the value through it. &mut T is a mutable reference. At any moment, a value can have many &T or one &mut T, never both. A borrow ends after its last use, not at the closing brace. Example: let mut v = vec![1, 2]; let first = &v[0]; println!(\"{first}\"); v.push(3); compiles, because first's last use comes before the push.","items":[{"type":"mcq","q":"Which combination of references to one value is allowed at the same time?","options":["Two &T shared references","One &T and one &mut T","Two &mut T mutable references","A &mut T and a second &mut T in a different scope that overlaps"],"answer":"Two &T shared references","why":"Many shared references are allowed, but a mutable reference cannot coexist with any other reference to the same value."},{"type":"mcq","q":"What must be true before let r = &mut x; compiles?","options":["x must be declared with let mut","x must already be a reference","x must be cloned first","x must be a Vec or String"],"answer":"x must be declared with let mut","why":"Creating a mutable reference requires the underlying variable to be declared mutable."},{"type":"mcq","q":"Why does calling v.push() conflict with holding a reference like &v[0]?","options":["push may reallocate and move the elements","push deletes the first element","push takes a runtime lock on v","push changes the type of v"],"answer":"push may reallocate and move the elements","why":"If the vector reallocates, the existing reference would point to freed memory, so the compiler forbids the overlap."},{"type":"mcq","q":"When does a borrow end?","options":["After its last use","At the closing brace of its scope","When the enclosing function returns","When the program exits"],"answer":"After its last use","why":"Rust uses non-lexical lifetimes, so a borrow stops once it is no longer used, even inside a larger scope."},{"type":"recall","q":"This code fails to compile: let first = &v[0]; v.push(4); println!(\"{first}\"); Describe a fix that keeps the same logic.","answer":"Use first before the push, so its last use ends before v.push(4). Alternatively, for an i32 element, copy the value with let first = v[0]; before pushing, since that stores a number rather than a borrow.","why":"Narrowing or reordering the borrow ends it before the conflicting mutation."},{"type":"recall","q":"Why can't a &T reference change the value it points to, and when does Rust check this rule?","answer":"&T grants only read access, and changing a value requires &mut T. The compiler verifies these rules before the program runs, so there is no runtime check cost.","why":"Shared references are read-only by design, and borrow checking happens entirely at compile time."}]}

{"learner":"Python-fluent developer (classes, dicts, asyncio) new to compiled languages; understands shared references, has a shaky intuition for move semantics, and has never seen a borrow checker. Goal: Rust from zero to production.","lessons":[{"id":"toolchain-cargo-hello","title":"Compiling Your First Rust Program with Cargo","explain":"Python runs source through an interpreter. Rust is compiled: rustc turns source into a native binary before it runs. Cargo is the tool that wraps rustc, manages dependencies, and runs tests. Run `cargo new hello` to create a project with src/main.rs and Cargo.toml. `cargo run` builds and executes it; `cargo build --release` produces an optimized binary in target/release. Example: main.rs contains `fn main() { println!(\"Hi\"); }`, and `cargo run` prints Hi after compiling. Compile errors appear before any code runs.","items":[{"type":"mcq","q":"What does Cargo do that plain rustc does not?","options":["Manages dependencies, builds, and tests projects","Converts Rust to Python","Runs code in an interpreter","Replaces the compiler"],"answer":"Manages dependencies, builds, and tests projects","why":"Cargo is the build tool and package manager that calls rustc for you."},{"type":"mcq","q":"Which command creates a new project named app?","options":["cargo init app.rs","cargo new app","rustc new app","cargo create --run app"],"answer":"cargo new app","why":"`cargo new` scaffolds Cargo.toml and src/main.rs."},{"type":"mcq","q":"Where does `cargo build --release` place the binary?","options":["src/release","target/release","bin/","build/"],"answer":"target/release","why":"Cargo writes build output to target/, with release builds in target/release."},{"type":"mcq","q":"Compared with Python, when are type and syntax errors in Rust reported?","options":["Only when that line runs","Only in production","Before the program runs, at compile time","Never, Rust ignores them"],"answer":"Before the program runs, at compile time","why":"Compilation must succeed before a binary exists to run."},{"type":"recall","q":"Which command compiles and runs your project in one step?","answer":"cargo run","why":"It builds if needed and then executes the binary."},{"type":"recall","q":"Which file lists a Rust project's name, version, and dependencies?","answer":"Cargo.toml","why":"It is the manifest, similar to pyproject.toml or requirements.txt combined."}]},{"id":"variables-mutability","title":"Variables, Immutability, and Shadowing","explain":"In Rust, variables are immutable by default. `let x = 5;` cannot be reassigned. Add `mut` to allow change: `let mut count = 0; count += 1;`. Shadowing lets you redeclare a name with `let`, even changing its type: `let s = \"42\"; let s: i32 = s.parse().unwrap();`. Constants use `const MAX: u32 = 100;` and require a type annotation. Unlike Python, where every name can be rebound freely, Rust makes mutation an explicit, visible choice, which helps the compiler and readers reason about code.","items":[{"type":"mcq","q":"What happens with `let x = 1; x = 2;`?","options":["x becomes 2","Compile error: cannot assign twice to immutable variable","x is shadowed","Runtime panic"],"answer":"Compile error: cannot assign twice to immutable variable","why":"Bindings are immutable unless declared with mut."},{"type":"mcq","q":"Which declaration allows `n += 1` later?","options":["let n = 0;","const n = 0;","let mut n = 0;","var n = 0;"],"answer":"let mut n = 0;","why":"`mut` marks the binding as mutable."},{"type":"mcq","q":"What does shadowing allow that `mut` does not?","options":["Changing a variable's type via a new `let`","Skipping initialization","Global scope","Faster code always"],"answer":"Changing a variable's type via a new `let`","why":"A new `let` creates a new variable, so its type may differ."},{"type":"mcq","q":"Which is true of `const`?","options":["It can be mut","It needs no type","It requires a type annotation","It is runtime only"],"answer":"It requires a type annotation","why":"Constants must be explicitly typed and be compile-time values."},{"type":"recall","q":"What keyword makes a Rust variable changeable?","answer":"mut","why":"Without it, the binding is immutable."},{"type":"recall","q":"Write a line that shadows `x` as its own value doubled, given `let x = 4;`.","answer":"let x = x * 2;","why":"A new `let` creates a fresh binding named x using the old value."}]},{"id":"scalar-types-functions","title":"Types and Functions","explain":"Rust is statically typed. Integers are explicit: i32, u8, i64, usize. Floats are f32 and f64. Also bool and char (a Unicode scalar, in single quotes). Functions declare parameter and return types: `fn add(a: i32, b: i32) -> i32 { a + b }`. The last expression without a semicolon is the return value; adding a semicolon turns it into a statement returning (). Unlike Python ints, Rust integers have fixed size and can overflow, so choose types deliberately.","items":[{"type":"mcq","q":"What does `fn f(a: i32) -> i32 { a + 1 }` return for f(2)?","options":["2","3","()","Compile error"],"answer":"3","why":"The final expression `a + 1` without a semicolon is returned."},{"type":"mcq","q":"What happens if you write `a + 1;` with a semicolon as the last line of that function?","options":["Returns a+1 still","Compile error: mismatched types, got ()","Returns 0","Runs but warns only"],"answer":"Compile error: mismatched types, got ()","why":"The semicolon makes it a statement, so the function returns () instead of i32."},{"type":"mcq","q":"Which type is unsigned and 8 bits?","options":["i8","u8","u16","f8"],"answer":"u8","why":"u means unsigned; 8 is the bit width."},{"type":"mcq","q":"How does Rust's integer differ from Python's int?","options":["It is fixed size and can overflow","It is unlimited size","It is always floating","It is dynamically typed"],"answer":"It is fixed size and can overflow","why":"Rust ints have set widths; Python ints grow arbitrarily."},{"type":"recall","q":"What symbol introduces a function's return type?","answer":"->","why":"Syntax is `fn name() -> Type`."},{"type":"recall","q":"What is the type of 'a' (single quotes) in Rust?","answer":"char","why":"Single quotes denote a char; double quotes denote a string."}]},{"id":"control-flow","title":"Control Flow as Expressions","explain":"`if` in Rust is an expression, so it can produce a value: `let label = if n > 0 { \"pos\" } else { \"neg\" };`. Conditions must be bool; there is no truthiness like Python's empty list. Loops: `loop` (infinite, can `break value`), `while cond`, and `for i in 0..5` (range excludes 5; `0..=5` includes it). Braces replace indentation. Example: `for i in 0..3 { println!(\"{i}\"); }` prints 0, 1, 2.","items":[{"type":"mcq","q":"What does `for i in 0..3` iterate over?","options":["0,1,2,3","1,2,3","0,1,2","0,1"],"answer":"0,1,2","why":"The range `a..b` excludes b."},{"type":"mcq","q":"Which is valid Rust?","options":["if 1 { }","if x > 0 { }","if [] { }","if \"a\" { }"],"answer":"if x > 0 { }","why":"Conditions must be bool; no truthiness."},{"type":"mcq","q":"What does `let v = if true { 1 } else { 2 };` give v?","options":["1","2","true","Compile error"],"answer":"1","why":"`if` is an expression and yields the chosen branch's value."},{"type":"mcq","q":"Which loop can return a value via break?","options":["while","for","loop","none"],"answer":"loop","why":"`break value;` works inside `loop`."},{"type":"recall","q":"Which range syntax includes the upper bound 5?","answer":"0..=5","why":"`..=` is inclusive."},{"type":"recall","q":"Name the keyword for an infinite loop in Rust.","answer":"loop","why":"`loop { }` runs until break."}]},{"id":"ownership-moves","title":"Ownership and Moves","explain":"Every value in Rust has exactly one owner. When the owner goes out of scope, the value is dropped and its memory freed, with no garbage collector. Assigning a heap value like String to another variable moves it: `let a = String::from(\"hi\"); let b = a;` now a is invalid, and using it is a compile error. This differs from Python, where both names would share the object. Simple fixed-size types like i32 implement Copy, so `let y = x;` leaves x usable. To duplicate a String deliberately, call `.clone()`.","items":[{"type":"mcq","q":"After `let a = String::from(\"hi\"); let b = a;`, what about `println!(\"{a}\")`?","options":["Prints hi","Compile error: value moved","Prints empty","Runtime error"],"answer":"Compile error: value moved","why":"Ownership moved to b, so a is no longer valid."},{"type":"mcq","q":"Why does `let y = x;` keep x valid when x is i32?","options":["i32 implements Copy","i32 is heap allocated","Rust ignores it","i32 is a reference"],"answer":"i32 implements Copy","why":"Copy types are duplicated bitwise instead of moved."},{"type":"mcq","q":"When is a value dropped?","options":["When its owner goes out of scope","At program exit only","When a GC runs","Never automatically"],"answer":"When its owner goes out of scope","why":"Rust frees memory deterministically at scope end."},{"type":"mcq","q":"How do you make an independent copy of a String?","options":["let b = a;","a.clone()","&a","a.move()"],"answer":"a.clone()","why":"`clone` performs an explicit deep copy."},{"type":"recall","q":"How many owners can a Rust value have at a time?","answer":"One","why":"Single ownership is the core rule enabling safe automatic freeing."},{"type":"recall","q":"What trait lets a type be duplicated implicitly on assignment?","answer":"Copy","why":"Types like integers implement Copy so assignment does not move them."}]},{"id":"ownership-functions","title":"Moves into Functions and Returns","explain":"Passing a value to a function moves it, just like assignment. `fn take(s: String) {}` called as `take(name);` means name is unusable afterward, since take owns it and drops it at its end. A function can give ownership back by returning the value: `fn give() -> String { String::from(\"x\") }`. Returning ownership back and forth is clumsy, which is why Rust has borrowing, covered next. Copy types such as i32 are copied into functions, so the caller keeps using them.","items":[{"type":"mcq","q":"After `take(name);` where take(s: String), can you use name?","options":["Yes","No, it was moved","Only if mut","Only in loops"],"answer":"No, it was moved","why":"Passing by value transfers ownership to the function."},{"type":"mcq","q":"Passing an i32 to `fn f(n: i32)` leaves the caller's variable...","options":["Invalid","Usable, because it was copied","Dropped","Borrowed"],"answer":"Usable, because it was copied","why":"i32 is Copy."},{"type":"mcq","q":"When is the String param s dropped in `fn take(s: String) {}`?","options":["When take ends","At program exit","Never","When caller ends"],"answer":"When take ends","why":"The function owns s, so it is dropped at the end of its scope."},{"type":"mcq","q":"How can a function hand ownership back to the caller?","options":["Return the value","Use mut","Call drop twice","Use const"],"answer":"Return the value","why":"Returning moves ownership out to the caller."},{"type":"recall","q":"What happens to ownership when you pass a String by value to a function?","answer":"It moves into the function","why":"The caller loses access unless it is returned."},{"type":"recall","q":"Which feature, covered next, avoids moving values in and out of functions?","answer":"Borrowing (references)","why":"References let functions use values without taking ownership."}]},{"id":"borrowing-references","title":"Borrowing with References","explain":"A reference lets you use a value without owning it. `&s` creates a shared (immutable) borrow; `&mut s` creates a mutable borrow. Example: `fn len(s: &String) -> usize { s.len() }` called as `len(&name)` leaves name usable. The borrow checker enforces: any number of `&` references OR exactly one `&mut` at a time, never both. This prevents data races and Python-style surprises where one alias mutates data another is reading. References must never outlive their owner.","items":[{"type":"mcq","q":"What does `&s` create?","options":["A move","A shared immutable borrow","A copy","A mutable borrow"],"answer":"A shared immutable borrow","why":"`&` borrows without taking ownership or permitting mutation."},{"type":"mcq","q":"Which combination is allowed at one time?","options":["Two &mut to same value","One &mut and one &","Many & references","None of these"],"answer":"Many & references","why":"Multiple shared borrows are fine; mutable access must be exclusive."},{"type":"mcq","q":"After `len(&name)`, can you use name?","options":["No, moved","Yes, only borrowed","Only after clone","Only if const"],"answer":"Yes, only borrowed","why":"Borrowing leaves ownership with the caller."},{"type":"mcq","q":"What does the borrow checker prevent?","options":["Aliased mutation and dangling references","Printing","Using loops","Defining functions"],"answer":"Aliased mutation and dangling references","why":"It enforces exclusivity of mutation and valid lifetimes of references at compile time."},{"type":"recall","q":"What is the syntax for a mutable reference to s?","answer":"&mut s","why":"The value must also be declared `let mut s`."},{"type":"recall","q":"State the rule for & and &mut references at one time.","answer":"Many & or exactly one &mut, not both","why":"This exclusivity guarantees no data races or invalidated reads."}]},{"id":"strings-slices","title":"String vs &str and Slices","explain":"Rust has two main string types. `String` is an owned, growable heap string. `&str` is a borrowed view into string data, such as a literal \"hello\". Create a String with `String::from(\"hi\")` or `\"hi\".to_string()`, and grow it with `push_str`. Slices borrow part of a sequence: `let w = &s[0..2];`. Prefer `&str` for function parameters, since it accepts both literals and `&String`. Strings are UTF-8, so you cannot index by integer like Python's `s[0]`.","items":[{"type":"mcq","q":"Which type owns its heap data and can grow?","options":["&str","String","char","&[u8]"],"answer":"String","why":"String is owned and growable."},{"type":"mcq","q":"What is the type of the literal \"hello\"?","options":["String","&str","str","char"],"answer":"&str","why":"Literals are borrowed string slices with static lifetime."},{"type":"mcq","q":"Why prefer `&str` parameters?","options":["Accepts literals and &String","Faster to type only","Allows mutation","Required by Cargo"],"answer":"Accepts literals and &String","why":"&String auto-converts to &str, so one signature serves both."},{"type":"mcq","q":"Why does `s[0]` fail on a String?","options":["Strings are UTF-8, so byte indexing is ambiguous","Indexes start at 1","Strings are immutable","It is a typo"],"answer":"Strings are UTF-8, so byte indexing is ambiguous","why":"A character may span multiple bytes, so integer indexing is disallowed."},{"type":"recall","q":"Which method appends a &str to a mutable String?","answer":"push_str","why":"`s.push_str(\"abc\")` extends the string."},{"type":"recall","q":"Write a slice of s covering its first 3 bytes.","answer":"&s[0..3]","why":"A range inside brackets, prefixed with &, borrows that portion."}]},{"id":"structs-methods","title":"Structs and Methods","explain":"A struct groups named fields, like a Python class with only data. `struct User { name: String, age: u32 }`. Behavior goes in an `impl` block: `impl User { fn greet(&self) -> String { format!(\"Hi {}\", self.name) } }`. `&self` borrows the instance, `&mut self` borrows mutably, and `self` consumes it. Associated functions without self, like `fn new(name: String) -> User`, are called as `User::new(...)`. There is no inheritance; sharing behavior uses traits, introduced later.","items":[{"type":"mcq","q":"Where do a struct's methods go?","options":["Inside the struct braces","In an impl block","In Cargo.toml","In a class"],"answer":"In an impl block","why":"Methods are defined separately in `impl TypeName { }`."},{"type":"mcq","q":"What does `&self` mean in a method?","options":["Method consumes the instance","Method borrows the instance immutably","Method is static","Method copies it"],"answer":"Method borrows the instance immutably","why":"`&self` is shorthand for `self: &Self`."},{"type":"mcq","q":"How do you call an associated function `new` on User?","options":["User.new()","User::new()","new(User)","user->new()"],"answer":"User::new()","why":"Associated functions use the `::` path syntax."},{"type":"mcq","q":"Which method receiver lets a method modify fields?","options":["&self","self: Copy","&mut self","const self"],"answer":"&mut self","why":"A mutable borrow is needed to change fields."},{"type":"recall","q":"Does Rust have class inheritance?","answer":"No","why":"Rust shares behavior through traits and composition instead."},{"type":"recall","q":"Which receiver takes ownership of the instance, consuming it?","answer":"self","why":"Plain `self` moves the instance into the method."}]},{"id":"enums-option-match","title":"Enums, Option, and match","explain":"Rust enums can carry data in each variant: `enum Shape { Circle(f64), Rect(f64, f64) }`. `match` handles every variant and the compiler enforces exhaustiveness. Rust has no None-like null; absence is `Option<T>`, either `Some(value)` or `None`. Example: `match find() { Some(n) => println!(\"{n}\"), None => println!(\"none\") }`. This replaces Python's `None` surprises: you cannot use an Option's value without handling the None case. `if let Some(n) = opt { }` is a shorter form for one case.","items":[{"type":"mcq","q":"What does Rust use instead of null?","options":["Option<T>","nil","undefined","0"],"answer":"Option<T>","why":"Option makes possible absence explicit in the type."},{"type":"mcq","q":"What does match exhaustiveness require?","options":["Every possible variant is handled","Only the first variant","A default always","No else"],"answer":"Every possible variant is handled","why":"The compiler rejects a match that misses cases."},{"type":"mcq","q":"Which is a valid Option value?","options":["Null","Some(3)","Maybe(3)","Ok(3)"],"answer":"Some(3)","why":"Option has variants Some(T) and None."},{"type":"mcq","q":"Which syntax handles just the Some case concisely?","options":["if let Some(n) = opt { }","while None","for Some","try Some"],"answer":"if let Some(n) = opt { }","why":"`if let` matches one pattern and ignores the rest."},{"type":"recall","q":"Name the two variants of Option<T>.","answer":"Some and None","why":"Some(T) holds a value; None means absence."},{"type":"recall","q":"What keyword branches on an enum's variants exhaustively?","answer":"match","why":"The compiler checks all variants are covered."}]},{"id":"result-error-handling","title":"Result and the ? Operator","explain":"Rust has no exceptions. Fallible functions return `Result<T, E>`, either `Ok(value)` or `Err(error)`. Example: `\"42\".parse::<i32>()` returns `Ok(42)`, while `\"x\".parse::<i32>()` returns `Err(..)`. You can `match` on it, or use `?` inside a function that itself returns Result: `let n: i32 = s.parse()?;` returns the error early if it fails. `unwrap()` panics on Err, so reserve it for tests and prototypes. `panic!` is for unrecoverable bugs, not normal errors.","items":[{"type":"mcq","q":"What does a fallible Rust function typically return?","options":["Result<T, E>","Throws exception","null","Option only"],"answer":"Result<T, E>","why":"Errors are values encoded in the return type."},{"type":"mcq","q":"What does `?` do on an Err?","options":["Ignores it","Returns the error early from the function","Panics always","Retries"],"answer":"Returns the error early from the function","why":"`?` propagates Err to the caller, unwrapping Ok otherwise."},{"type":"mcq","q":"What does `unwrap()` do on an Err?","options":["Returns default","Panics","Returns None","Logs only"],"answer":"Panics","why":"It crashes the thread, so avoid it in production paths."},{"type":"mcq","q":"Where can you use `?` on a Result?","options":["In any function","In a function returning a compatible Result or Option","Only in main without return","Only in loops"],"answer":"In a function returning a compatible Result or Option","why":"`?` needs a return type that can carry the propagated error."},{"type":"recall","q":"What are the two variants of Result?","answer":"Ok and Err","why":"Ok(T) holds success; Err(E) holds the error."},{"type":"recall","q":"Does Rust use exceptions for ordinary errors?","answer":"No","why":"It uses Result values; panic! is reserved for unrecoverable bugs."}]}]}

{"learner":"Adult beginner in Spanish, fluent in English, Gujarati and Hindi. Works with a client from Peru, so workplace conversation with coworkers comes first. Knows hola and ¿cómo estás?. Fix: 'Mi llamo' should be 'Me llamo', 'estu' should be 'estoy', and mañana means tomorrow, not today.","lessons":[
{"id":"greetings-by-time","title":"Greetings for Any Time of Day","explain":"Spanish greetings change with the time of day: Buenos días (morning), Buenas tardes (afternoon), Buenas noches (evening and night). Spanish vowels are pure, as in Hindi and Gujarati: a, e, i, o, u always sound the same. The letter h is silent, so hola sounds like 'OH-la'. Example: Buenos días. ¿Cómo estás? Bien, gracias, ¿y tú?","items":[
{"type":"mcq","q":"Which greeting fits 9 a.m. at the office?","options":["Buenos días","Buenas tardes","Buenas noches","Hasta luego"],"answer":"Buenos días","why":"Buenos días is used in the morning."},
{"type":"mcq","q":"How is the h in hola pronounced?","options":["It is silent","Like English h","Like k","Like j"],"answer":"It is silent","why":"Spanish h is silent, so hola sounds like 'OH-la'."},
{"type":"mcq","q":"A coworker says '¿Cómo estás?'. What are they asking?","options":["How are you?","What is your name?","Where are you?","What time is it?"],"answer":"How are you?","why":"¿Cómo estás? means 'How are you?'."},
{"type":"mcq","q":"Which reply answers politely and asks back?","options":["Bien, gracias, ¿y tú?","Buenas noches, adiós","Me llamo bien","Hola, hola"],"answer":"Bien, gracias, ¿y tú?","why":"It means 'Fine, thanks, and you?'."},
{"type":"recall","q":"Say 'Good afternoon' in Spanish.","answer":"Buenas tardes","why":"Tardes covers the afternoon and early evening."},
{"type":"recall","q":"Say 'And you?' (informal) in Spanish.","answer":"¿Y tú?","why":"Y means 'and' and tú means 'you' (informal)."}]},
{"id":"saying-your-name","title":"Saying Your Name","explain":"To give your name, say Me llamo plus your name. It literally means 'I call myself'. Me is 'myself' and mi is 'my', so 'Mi llamo' is a common mistake. You can also say Soy plus your name, meaning 'I am'. After meeting someone, say Mucho gusto (nice to meet you). Example: Me llamo Alex. Mucho gusto.","items":[
{"type":"mcq","q":"Which sentence is correct?","options":["Me llamo Alex","Mi llamo Alex","Me llama Alex","Yo llamo Alex"],"answer":"Me llamo Alex","why":"Use me (myself) with llamo, not mi (my)."},
{"type":"mcq","q":"What does 'Mucho gusto' mean?","options":["Nice to meet you","Thank you very much","Good morning","See you later"],"answer":"Nice to meet you","why":"Mucho gusto is the standard phrase when meeting someone."},
{"type":"mcq","q":"Which sentence means 'I am Alex'?","options":["Soy Alex","Estás Alex","Se llama Alex","Es Alex"],"answer":"Soy Alex","why":"Soy is the 'I am' form of ser."},
{"type":"mcq","q":"A coworker asks '¿Cómo te llamas?'. What do they want to know?","options":["Your name","Your job","Your mood","Your city"],"answer":"Your name","why":"¿Cómo te llamas? means 'What is your name?'."},
{"type":"recall","q":"Say 'My name is Priya.' using llamarse.","answer":"Me llamo Priya","why":"Soy Priya is also correct, but the target here is Me llamo."},
{"type":"recall","q":"Say 'Nice to meet you.'","answer":"Mucho gusto","why":"Literally 'much pleasure'."}]},
{"id":"estoy-how-i-feel","title":"Estoy: How You Feel Right Now","explain":"To say how you feel now, use estar. The forms are yo estoy, tú estás, él/ella está. Spanish usually drops yo, so say Estoy bien. The word is estoy, never 'estu'. Useful words: bien (fine), cansado (tired), ocupado (busy). Use -a for a woman: cansada, ocupada. Example: Estoy ocupado, pero estoy bien.","items":[
{"type":"mcq","q":"Which means 'I am tired'?","options":["Estoy cansado","Estu cansado","Estás cansado","Está cansado"],"answer":"Estoy cansado","why":"Estoy is the 'I' form of estar; 'estu' does not exist."},
{"type":"mcq","q":"How do you say 'You are fine' to a coworker (informal)?","options":["Estás bien","Estoy bien","Estamos bien","Están bien"],"answer":"Estás bien","why":"Estás is the informal 'you' form."},
{"type":"mcq","q":"What does 'ocupado' mean?","options":["Busy","Tired","Happy","Late"],"answer":"Busy","why":"Ocupado is the same root as 'occupied'."},
{"type":"mcq","q":"Complete: '___ muy bien, gracias.'","options":["Estoy","Estu","Estar","Estás"],"answer":"Estoy","why":"The speaker is 'I', so estoy."},
{"type":"recall","q":"Say 'I am busy.'","answer":"Estoy ocupado","why":"Women say Estoy ocupada."},
{"type":"recall","q":"Say 'I am fine.'","answer":"Estoy bien","why":"Estoy plus bien."}]},
{"id":"hoy-manana-ayer","title":"Today, Tomorrow, Yesterday","explain":"Hoy means today, mañana means tomorrow, and ayer means yesterday. Careful: mañana can also mean 'morning', as in por la mañana (in the morning). When it stands alone as a day word, it means tomorrow, never today. Example: Hoy estoy ocupado; mañana estoy libre. (Libre means free.)","items":[
{"type":"mcq","q":"As a day word, what does 'mañana' mean?","options":["Tomorrow","Today","Yesterday","Tonight"],"answer":"Tomorrow","why":"Mañana is tomorrow. Today is hoy."},
{"type":"mcq","q":"Which word means 'today'?","options":["Hoy","Ayer","Mañana","Libre"],"answer":"Hoy","why":"Hoy is today."},
{"type":"mcq","q":"Which sentence means 'Today I am tired'?","options":["Hoy estoy cansado","Mañana estoy cansado","Ayer estoy cansado","Hoy estás cansado"],"answer":"Hoy estoy cansado","why":"Hoy is today and estoy is 'I am'."},
{"type":"mcq","q":"What does 'por la mañana' mean?","options":["In the morning","Tomorrow night","Yesterday","Every day"],"answer":"In the morning","why":"Mañana also means morning in this phrase."},
{"type":"recall","q":"Say 'yesterday' in Spanish.","answer":"ayer","why":"Ayer is yesterday."},
{"type":"recall","q":"Say 'Tomorrow I am free.'","answer":"Mañana estoy libre","why":"Mañana is tomorrow and libre is free."}]},
{"id":"when-you-dont-understand","title":"When You Don't Understand","explain":"Beginners need rescue phrases. Say No entiendo (I don't understand). Ask ¿Puedes repetir, por favor? (Can you repeat, please?). Ask for slower speech with Más despacio, por favor. To learn a word, ask ¿Cómo se dice...? (How do you say...?). Example: ¿Cómo se dice 'meeting' en español?","items":[
{"type":"mcq","q":"What does 'No entiendo' mean?","options":["I don't understand","I don't know you","I am not here","I am not busy"],"answer":"I don't understand","why":"No means not, and entiendo means I understand."},
{"type":"mcq","q":"How do you ask someone to speak more slowly?","options":["Más despacio, por favor","Más tarde, por favor","Otra vez, adiós","No gracias"],"answer":"Más despacio, por favor","why":"Despacio means slowly."},
{"type":"mcq","q":"What does '¿Puedes repetir?' mean?","options":["Can you repeat?","Can you help?","Can you wait?","Can you call?"],"answer":"Can you repeat?","why":"Repetir means to repeat."},
{"type":"mcq","q":"Which asks 'How do you say meeting in Spanish?'","options":["¿Cómo se dice 'meeting' en español?","¿Cómo estás 'meeting' en español?","¿Dónde se llama 'meeting'?","¿Qué es mañana?"],"answer":"¿Cómo se dice 'meeting' en español?","why":"¿Cómo se dice...? is the standard way to ask for a word."},
{"type":"recall","q":"Say 'I don't understand.'","answer":"No entiendo","why":"No plus entiendo."},
{"type":"recall","q":"Say 'Slower, please.'","answer":"Más despacio, por favor","why":"Más despacio means 'more slowly'."}]},
{"id":"polite-words","title":"Polite Words for the Office","explain":"Polite words keep coworkers friendly. Por favor means please and gracias means thanks. Muchas gracias is thank you very much, and the reply is De nada (you're welcome). Say Perdón or Disculpa to apologize. Say Con permiso to pass by someone or enter a space. Example: Gracias. De nada.","items":[
{"type":"mcq","q":"What does 'De nada' mean?","options":["You're welcome","Good night","Excuse me","See you soon"],"answer":"You're welcome","why":"It is the usual reply to gracias."},
{"type":"mcq","q":"You need to squeeze past a coworker in the hallway. What do you say?","options":["Con permiso","De nada","Mucho gusto","Hasta mañana"],"answer":"Con permiso","why":"Con permiso means 'with your permission' and is used to pass by."},
{"type":"mcq","q":"You bump into someone. What do you say?","options":["Perdón","Gracias","Buenas tardes","Por favor"],"answer":"Perdón","why":"Perdón is the quick apology."},
{"type":"mcq","q":"What does 'Muchas gracias' mean?","options":["Thank you very much","Please sit","Good morning","Nice to meet you"],"answer":"Thank you very much","why":"Mucho/muchas means much or many, so muchas gracias is 'many thanks'."},
{"type":"recall","q":"Say 'Thank you very much.'","answer":"Muchas gracias","why":"Muchas is used with the feminine gracias."},
{"type":"recall","q":"Say 'You're welcome.'","answer":"De nada","why":"Literally 'of nothing'."}]},
{"id":"where-are-you-from","title":"Where Are You From?","explain":"Use ser for who you are and where you are from. The forms are yo soy, tú eres, él/ella es. Ask ¿De dónde eres? (Where are you from?). Answer Soy de plus the place. Mi means my. Example: Soy de la India. Mi cliente es de Perú. Use estar for feelings and ser for origin: estoy cansado, but soy de la India.","items":[
{"type":"mcq","q":"What does '¿De dónde eres?' ask?","options":["Where are you from?","How are you?","What is your name?","What time is it?"],"answer":"Where are you from?","why":"De dónde means 'from where'."},
{"type":"mcq","q":"Which means 'I am from India'?","options":["Soy de la India","Estoy de la India","Soy en India","Eres de la India"],"answer":"Soy de la India","why":"Origin uses ser (soy) plus de."},
{"type":"mcq","q":"Which means 'My client is from Peru'?","options":["Mi cliente es de Perú","Mi cliente está de Perú","Mi cliente soy de Perú","Mi cliente eres de Perú"],"answer":"Mi cliente es de Perú","why":"Third person ser is es, and mi is 'my'."},
{"type":"mcq","q":"Which verb do you use to say where someone is from?","options":["ser (soy, eres, es)","estar (estoy, estás, está)","llamar (llamo, llamas)","hablar (hablo, hablas)"],"answer":"ser (soy, eres, es)","why":"Ser is used for identity and origin."},
{"type":"recall","q":"Ask a coworker 'Where are you from?' (informal).","answer":"¿De dónde eres?","why":"De dónde plus eres."},
{"type":"recall","q":"Say 'She is from Peru.'","answer":"Ella es de Perú","why":"Ella es means 'she is'."}]},
{"id":"work-words","title":"Work Words You Will Use Daily","explain":"Core office words: el cliente (client), la reunión (meeting), el correo (email), el proyecto (project), la oficina (office). Trabajo means 'I work'. Use con (with) and en (in or at). Example: Trabajo con un cliente de Perú. Trabajo en una oficina.","items":[
{"type":"mcq","q":"What does 'la reunión' mean?","options":["The meeting","The office","The email","The project"],"answer":"The meeting","why":"Reunión is a meeting or gathering."},
{"type":"mcq","q":"What does 'el correo' mean in a work chat?","options":["The email","The client","The lunch","The desk"],"answer":"The email","why":"Correo means mail, and is commonly used for email."},
{"type":"mcq","q":"Which means 'I work with a client'?","options":["Trabajo con un cliente","Trabajas con un cliente","Trabajamos con un cliente","Trabajan con un cliente"],"answer":"Trabajo con un cliente","why":"Trabajo is the 'I' form."},
{"type":"mcq","q":"Which word means 'project'?","options":["proyecto","oficina","cliente","reunión"],"answer":"proyecto","why":"Proyecto is a close cognate of 'project'."},
{"type":"recall","q":"Say 'the meeting' in Spanish.","answer":"la reunión","why":"Reunión is feminine, so la."},
{"type":"recall","q":"Say 'I work in an office.'","answer":"Trabajo en una oficina","why":"En means in or at, and oficina is feminine, so una."}]},
{"id":"numbers-and-meeting-time","title":"Numbers 1–10 and Meeting Times","explain":"Numbers: uno, dos, tres, cuatro, cinco, seis, siete, ocho, nueve, diez. To give a time, say a las plus the number. For one o'clock, say a la una. Ask ¿A qué hora es la reunión? (What time is the meeting?). Example: La reunión es a las tres.","items":[
{"type":"mcq","q":"Which number is 'cinco'?","options":["5","4","6","10"],"answer":"5","why":"Cinco is five."},
{"type":"mcq","q":"Which number is 'nueve'?","options":["9","7","8","1"],"answer":"9","why":"Nueve is nine."},
{"type":"mcq","q":"What does 'La reunión es a las cuatro' mean?","options":["The meeting is at four","The meeting is for four people","The meeting is on day four","The meeting is four hours long"],"answer":"The meeting is at four","why":"A las plus a number gives the time."},
{"type":"mcq","q":"What does '¿A qué hora es la reunión?' ask?","options":["What time is the meeting?","Where is the meeting?","Who is in the meeting?","When was the meeting?"],"answer":"What time is the meeting?","why":"Hora means hour or time."},
{"type":"recall","q":"Write the number 10 in Spanish.","answer":"diez","why":"Diez is ten."},
{"type":"recall","q":"Say 'The meeting is at two.'","answer":"La reunión es a las dos","why":"A las plus dos."}]},
